props.title: Destino

sections.content: Destino (2003) represents one of animation's most fascinating collaborations - a surreal marriage between Walt Disney and Salvador Dalí conceived in 1945 but completed 58 years later. The project began as a partnership between two visionary artists at their creative peaks, with Dalí working directly at Disney's studio. Though only 17 seconds of animation were completed in the 1940s, Roy Disney resurrected the project in 1999, working from Dalí's original storyboards and artwork. The result is a haunting 6-minute meditation that perfectly captures Dalí's signature melting clocks, transforming figures, and dreamlike symbolism through fluid animation.

sections.content: Destino sits within a rich tradition of surrealist animation that includes pioneering works like The Adventures of Prince Achmed (1926) by Lotte Reiniger and Un Chien Andalou (1929) by Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí. Modern experimental animators continue pushing boundaries - Mind Game (2004) by Masaaki Yuasa and Waking Life (2001) by Richard Linklater use animation to explore consciousness and reality in ways that echo Destino's dreamlike quality.

The film's production history bridges animation's hand-drawn golden age and its digital renaissance. While maintaining Dalí's artistic vision, the completion team used computer animation to achieve effects that would have been nearly impossible in the 1940s. This hybrid approach influenced later experimental shorts like The Mysterious Geographic Explorations of Jasper Morello (2005) and Madagascar, a Journey Diary (2009). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: Destino's delayed completion ironically positioned it to influence 21st century animation more than if it had been released in the 1940s. Its techniques for translating surrealist art into motion can be seen in films like Paprika (2006) and The Congress (2013). The project also demonstrated Disney's willingness to embrace experimental animation, paving the way for shorts like Lorenzo (2004) and Inner Workings (2016).
